items.followUp: How can a supersaturated solution be prepared from a saturated solution?

rubric.why: Award for describing the preparation method.
rubric.description: Heat the saturated solution and then cool it slowly.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for heating followed by slow cooling.

rubric.why: Award for stating what makes the cooled solution supersaturated.
rubric.description: On cooling, more solute remains dissolved than the solution can normally hold at that temperature.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for stating that excess solute remains dissolved or that the solution is supersaturated.

modelAnswer: Heat a saturated solution so that more solute dissolves in it.
Cool the solution slowly and without disturbing it; the excess solute remains dissolved, forming a supersaturated solution.
A supersaturated solution is unstable, so adding a crystal of solute may cause the excess solute to crystallize out.

rubric.why: The textbook definition identifies oxidation by oxygen addition or hydrogen removal.
rubric.description: Oxidation is the addition of oxygen to a substance or the removal of hydrogen from it.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for either textbook criterion.

rubric.why: Electron loss is the modern definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: In terms of electrons, oxidation is the loss of electrons.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the electron-based definition.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is a chemical reaction in which oxygen is added to a substance or hydrogen is removed from it.
In terms of electrons, oxidation is the loss of electrons.

items.followUp: What is an alloy? Give one example.

rubric.why: Alloying involves combining a metal with another element or elements.
rubric.description: Alloying is the process of mixing a metal with one or more other elements.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the mixing or combining process.

rubric.why: Alloying is commonly carried out by melting the components together to form an alloy.
rubric.description: The components are melted and mixed to form an alloy.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for identifying the molten mixing or the alloy formed.

modelAnswer: Alloying is the process of mixing a metal with one or more other elements, usually by melting them together.
The mixture formed is called an alloy.

items.followUp: Name and describe four other branches of Chemistry.

rubric.why: A correct branch name with its subject earns credit.
rubric.description: Names and briefly describes one valid branch of Chemistry.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for each correctly named branch with a suitable description; accept any four.

modelAnswer: Physical chemistry deals with the laws and principles governing the properties and behaviour of matter.
Organic chemistry deals with carbon compounds, especially hydrocarbons and their derivatives.
Inorganic chemistry deals with the properties and reactions of elements and their compounds, except most carbon compounds.
Biochemistry deals with the chemical substances and reactions occurring in living organisms.

items.followUp: Explain why water molecules attract one another through hydrogen bonding.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding is an attraction between molecules, not a covalent bond within one molecule.
rubric.description: Identify hydrogen bonding as an intermolecular force of attraction.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for identifying it as an intermolecular attraction.

rubric.why: Hydrogen bonding occurs when hydrogen is bonded to a highly electronegative atom such as F, O, or N.
rubric.description: State that the hydrogen atom is bonded to a highly electronegative atom, such as fluorine, oxygen or nitrogen.
rubric.how: Give up to 2 marks for the hydrogen-to-electronegative-atom condition and a correct example.

rubric.why: The hydrogen is attracted to an electronegative atom on a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.description: Explain that hydrogen is attracted to an electronegative atom, often described as its lone pair, in a neighbouring molecule.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the neighbouring-molecule attraction.

rubric.why: Water provides a familiar example of hydrogen bonding between molecules.
rubric.description: Give water as an example of molecules that form hydrogen bonds.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for a correct example such as water.

modelAnswer: Hydrogen bonding is a special intermolecular force of attraction between molecules.
It occurs when a hydrogen atom bonded to a highly electronegative atom, such as oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, is attracted to an electronegative atom in a neighbouring molecule.
The attraction is between molecules and is weaker than the covalent bond within each molecule.
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another.
Hydrogen bonding helps account for water's unusually high boiling point compared with similar small molecules.

items.followUp: State four physical properties of metals and non-metals.

rubric.why: Lustre is a standard contrasting physical property.
rubric.description: Metals are generally lustrous, whereas non-metals are generally dull.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Malleability and brittleness distinguish many metals from solid non-metals.
rubric.description: Metals are generally malleable and ductile, while solid non-metals are generally brittle.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Conductivity is a key physical difference between the groups.
rubric.description: Metals generally conduct heat and electricity well; non-metals generally conduct them poorly.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct contrast.

rubric.why: Sonority is another standard physical property of metals.
rubric.description: Metals are generally sonorous; non-metals are generally non-sonorous.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the correct contrast.

modelAnswer: Metals are generally lustrous, whereas non-metals are generally dull.
Metals are generally malleable and ductile, whereas solid non-metals are generally brittle.
Metals are generally good conductors of heat and electricity, whereas non-metals are generally poor conductors.
Metals are generally sonorous, whereas non-metals are generally non-sonorous.

items.followUp: The empirical formula of a compound is CH₂ and its molar mass is 42 g mol⁻¹. Find its molecular formula.

rubric.why: The definition states what the empirical formula represents.
rubric.description: A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule; the empirical formula gives their simplest whole-number ratio.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for correctly defining the molecular formula in relation to the empirical formula.

accept: n= molecular mass/ empirical formula mass
rubric.why: The multiplier is calculated by dividing the molecular mass by the empirical formula mass.
rubric.description: The molecular formula is obtained by multiplying the empirical formula by n, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the multiplier relationship and method.

modelAnswer: The molecular formula shows the actual number of atoms of each element in one molecule of a compound.
It is derived from the empirical formula by multiplying all its subscripts by n, where n = molecular mass ÷ empirical formula mass.

items.followUp: Define one atomic mass unit and state its value in grams.

rubric.why: One atomic mass unit is defined relative to a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.description: One atomic mass unit is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for the carbon-12 definition.

rubric.why: Award for the accepted approximate value in grams.
rubric.description: State the value of one atomic mass unit in grams.
rubric.how: Give 1 mark for 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g, with an acceptable rounding.

modelAnswer: One atomic mass unit (u) is one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom.
